Meticulous

/muh-TIK-yuh-luhs/ - the stress falls on TIK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Meticulous means extremely careful about small details.

The wedding planner was meticulous about the seating plan, spacing the feuding cousins to the exact table.

Worked Example

The film was set in 1943, and the prop master furnished the detective's desk as if the camera might read it: a phone book printed for the right city and year, the half-smoked cigarette brand the script named, pencils sharpened to wartime length, a blotter aged with tea. None of it holds the shot for more than a second. All of it is there.

Meticulous is the exact word because the prop master is extremely careful about small details — care spent down at the grain of the work, where most eyes never go. This unit's fastidious describes the judge whom nothing satisfies; meticulous describes the maker who satisfies even that judge. The care is spent on the work itself, one small correct thing at a time.

How Meticulous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

precise

precise: exact in numbers and statements

thorough

thorough: covers everything once; meticulous lingers over the fine grain of each thing

Antonyms

careless

careless: lets details slip unexamined

slapdash

slapdash: rushed work, with the details left to fend for themselves

How Strong Is It? — careful → meticulous → fanatical

careful vs. meticulous

careful vs. meticulous: A careful cook checks the big things; a meticulous one logs the water temperature to the half degree.

fanatical vs. meticulous

fanatical vs. meticulous: Fanatical goes past meticulous — care swollen into creed, continued long after the details have stopped repaying it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — meticul

Root — meticul: fearful (Latin metus, 'fear,' via meticulosus)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Meticul- (fearful — Latin metus, "fear," stretched into meticulosus) + -ous (full of) = full of fear. The first meticulous people were literally fearful ones; the word crossed into English meaning "timid," then shrank to the craftsman's version of fear — working as if terrified that one small slip will spoil the whole. The fear dried out of it; the double-checking stayed.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin metus, "fear," built no other common English word — meticulous carries the root alone. Even its own original timid sense faded, leaving only the careful one.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / admiring

Meticulous is praise for care at the grain — the maker's virtue. Keep the family straight: this unit's fastidious describes the impossible-to-please judge, methodical the ordered steps, and scrupulous adds a conscience — a meticulous forger is entirely possible; a scrupulous one is a contradiction. When the wonder is how small the attended details are, meticulous.
